name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,696

clue.text: Aimless, wandering girl

indicators.note: something wandering strays from its set course, so these letters drift out of their order

blocks.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A girl drifting about without any purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aimless, wandering' reads as two adjectives describing the girl, but the first is the raw material and the second tells you to scramble it.
explanation.definitionFit: Melissa is a female given name, so it is one example of what a setter calls a girl.

clue.text: Rising corporation poaching American banker's design

indicators.note: a poacher takes something and keeps it inside his bag, so one part ends up holding others
in a down clue, rising means read from the bottom upwards, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a corporation is old humorous slang for a paunch, and tum is the stomach
standard abbreviation for American
a banker is something with banks, a river; the Po is Italy's longest river

explanation.surface: A business on the rise stealing a US bank's plans.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests finance, but 'banker' is the crossword's river and 'corporation' is a fat belly. The 's stands for 'is', joining wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To map out a scheme is to plan or lay it out in detail, which is the verb sense of design.

clue.text: Country that's ravaged vital area

indicators.note: something ravaged has been wrecked and torn apart, so these letters are left in a new jumble

blocks.note: taken as written
standard abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A nation whose vital region has been devastated by war.
explanation.walkthrough: Only 'vital' is taken whole; 'area' contributes just its abbreviation A to the letters being mixed.
explanation.definitionFit: Latvia is a Baltic state in northern Europe, so it fits the plain description of a sovereign nation.

clue.text: Aluminium driver taken below bunker, possibly, or tree

blocks.note: a golf bunker is a sand trap, and 'possibly' marks the indirect hint
Al is the chemical symbol for aluminium
a driver is a golf club of the kind traditionally called a wood

explanation.surface: A golfer's metal driver, taken beneath a bunker, with a tree as the alternative hazard.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, 'taken below' puts the aluminium and driver pieces underneath the bunker piece. The golf scene makes 'driver' a club, not a motorist.
explanation.definitionFit: Sandalwood is a fragrant tropical tree prized for its scented timber and oil.

clue.text: Phone company's partial withdrawal of help package

indicators.note: partial means only part of the phrase is used, so the letters sit inside the words
to withdraw is to pull back, so the letters are read going backwards

blocks.note: the run of letters straddling the two words, read forwards

explanation.surface: A telecoms firm partly pulling out of a support deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Withdrawal' sounds like a business retreat, but here it tells you to read the hidden letters backwards from the end of 'help' into 'package'.
explanation.definitionFit: Apple makes the iPhone, so the computing giant is fairly described as a maker of mobile handsets.

clue.text: Superficial cut in former Murdoch organisation

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it is placed inside, wrapped by the outer piece

blocks.note: Sky, the British satellite broadcaster, was controlled by Rupert Murdoch until 2018
to etch is to cut lines into a surface

explanation.surface: Job losses at a media company Rupert Murdoch used to own, described as only skin-deep.
explanation.walkthrough: Sky is the UK pay-TV broadcaster, sold by Murdoch's companies to Comcast in 2018. 'Cut' reads as a redundancy but means engraving.
explanation.definitionFit: Sketchy describes something lacking detail or depth, the same shallow quality as superficial treatment.

clue.text: Basked in a French club, having cast off clothing

indicators.note: clothing wraps a body, so the outer piece is put around the inner ones

blocks.note: to shed something is to cast it off, as a snake does its skin
un is the French for 'a'
a bat is a club for hitting a ball

explanation.surface: Someone lounged in the sun at a club in France after stripping off.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a French nightclub and nudity; in fact 'club' is a bat and 'clothing' wraps the past-tense shed around the French article and the bat.
explanation.definitionFit: To bask is to lie warming oneself in sunshine, which is exactly what someone who sunbathed did.

clue.text: Finally serve ace, then service finding net

indicators.note: finally points at the end, so only the closing letter of the word is used

blocks.note: the last letter of the word
A is the abbreviation for ace on playing cards
the Royal Navy is the Senior Service, abbreviated RN

explanation.surface: A tennis player at last serves an ace, then the next serve goes into the net.
explanation.walkthrough: The tennis scene hides the armed-services sense of 'service'; 'net' is the definition, a verb meaning to gain, not the tennis net.
explanation.definitionFit: To net a sum is to clear it as profit or wages, the same as to earn it.

clue.text: Rise to attend one brief encounter

indicators.note: something brief is cut short, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: to come up is to rise to a higher level
the word with its tail cut off

explanation.surface: Standing to be present at a short romantic meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief encounter' recalls the classic film, but 'brief' belongs to 'one'. 'To attend' simply places the shortened word beside the first piece.
explanation.definitionFit: To come upon someone is to meet or find them by chance, the verb sense of encounter.

clue.text: Ellen MacArthur's craft headed up island on blowy night

indicators.note: in a down entry, heading up means travelling from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards
something blowy is tossed about by wind, so the letters are scattered into a new order

blocks.note: a cay is a small low island or reef
taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A famous sailor's boat heads for an island on a windy night.
explanation.walkthrough: Ellen MacArthur is the British yachtswoman who set a solo round-the-world record in 2005. 'Craft' looks like a boat, but here means her skill.
explanation.definitionFit: Her craft in the sense of trade or skill is sailing, which in competitive form is yachting.

clue.text: Don's turned over in bed

indicators.note: turning something over flips it end to end, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: someone still in bed is not up yet

explanation.surface: A university fellow rolled over in his bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' looks like an Oxbridge lecturer, but it is the verb to don. 'In bed' must be rephrased as a two-word idea before being flipped.
explanation.definitionFit: To don clothes is to put them on, so the verb and the phrasal verb are synonyms.

clue.text: Wide-ranging terror grips soldiers by unwalled camp

indicators.note: removing the walls strips away the outer edges, leaving only the inside letters
to grip is to hold tightly, so one piece holds the others inside

blocks.note: panic is sudden overwhelming fear
OR stands for other ranks, soldiers who are not officers
the word without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Widespread fear seizes troops beside a camp with no defences.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' joins the soldiers to the trimmed camp, and that pair sits inside the terror word.
explanation.definitionFit: Panoramic means taking in a broad view or scope, so it describes something extensive and all-embracing.

clue.text: Redeveloped area until left by one side

indicators.note: redeveloping a site rebuilds it in a new layout, so the letters are rebuilt in another order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A neighbourhood was redeveloped and abandoned by one of the parties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' reads as abandoned, but it supplies just L to the mix; 'by one side' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A unilateral decision or action is taken or performed by just one party, without the agreement of others.

clue.text: Part of deck sees action

blocks.note: first meaning: one of the four sets in a pack of cards
second meaning: a case brought in a court of law

explanation.surface: Part of a ship's deck witnesses some activity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deck' suggests a ship, but it is a pack of cards; 'action' is the legal kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearts, clubs, diamonds and spades are the four groups of a card pack, and a lawsuit is a legal proceeding.

clue.text: Writer to yearn for goddess

blocks.note: a proser is a writer of prose
to pine is to long or yearn

explanation.surface: An author longing for a goddess.
explanation.walkthrough: PROSER is an uncommon word for a prose writer, often a dull one.
explanation.definitionFit: Proserpine is the Roman name of the deity of spring and queen of the underworld, the Greek Persephone.

clue.text: Like the Sphinx, reportedly, if accepted

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the sound counts rather than the spelling

blocks.note: 'whether' can stand for 'if'
in informal British use, to wear an idea is to accept or tolerate it

explanation.surface: A description of the Great Sphinx, said to hold if it is generally agreed.
explanation.walkthrough: Only 'if' is affected by the homophone; 'accepted' uses the British idiom 'he won't wear that', meaning he won't accept it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Great Sphinx at Giza has been eroded by thousands of years of wind and sand, so it is visibly worn by the elements.

clue.text: Ancient sea-creatures with shells, say, paladins picked up

indicators.note: to pick up a sound is to hear it, so the word is taken by how it is heard

blocks.note: shells are one kind of ammunition, informally ammo
paladins were the knights of Charlemagne's court

explanation.surface: Prehistoric marine animals with shells, as noticed by some medieval champions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shells' seems to belong with the sea creatures, but it is wordplay for ammunition; NITES is the informal spelling that sounds like the warriors.
explanation.definitionFit: Ammonites are extinct marine molluscs with coiled shells, common as fossils from the age of dinosaurs.

clue.text: Late for Lent?

blocks.note: first meaning: far on in time, as in an hour or age well along
second meaning: given as a loan, as a sum of money paid ahead

explanation.walkthrough: The capital L makes Lent look like the Christian fast, as if something is late for Easter; it is just the past tense of lend.
explanation.definitionFit: An advanced hour is a late one, and money advanced to someone has been loaned to them before it is earned.

clue.text: Sprinklers keep initially-trimmed grass high

indicators.note: trimming at the start cuts off the opening, so the word loses its first letter
someone high is intoxicated and muddled, so these letters lose their sober order

blocks.note: the word with its head cut off
taken as written

explanation.surface: Garden sprinklers keep freshly mown lawn standing tall.
explanation.walkthrough: The lawn picture makes 'high' describe the grass, but it is the anagram signal, as in drunk or drugged.
explanation.definitionFit: Asperges is the Catholic rite of sprinkling holy water, and the word also names the aspergillum used to scatter it.

clue.text: Brazen stripping after dance causes annoyance

indicators.note: stripping removes the outer covering, so only the inside letters are kept

blocks.note: a disco is a dance or dance party
brazen means immodest; that word without its outer letters

explanation.surface: Shameless undressing after a night of dancing upsets people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stripping' looks like the brazen act itself, but it tells you to peel the outer letters off the synonym IMMODEST.
explanation.definitionFit: To discommode someone is to inconvenience or trouble them, which is to cause them annoyance.

clue.text: Future queen, perhaps

blocks.note: surface reading: a royal heir, a princess waiting to take the throne
setter's reading: a queen is an adult female cat, so think of a young animal that may grow into one

explanation.walkthrough: The obvious reading is a princess; 'perhaps' hints that only a female youngster will become a queen.
explanation.definitionFit: A queen is the term for a breeding female cat, and a young female cat will grow into one.

clue.text: Rain ensues when Her Majesty attends event

blocks.note: a show is a public event or exhibition
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: It always rains when the Queen turns up at a public occasion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attends' places the royal letters beside the event, here after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A shower is a brief fall of rain, so the noun can stand for a spell of rain.

clue.text: Space age turned on first of Apollos

indicators.note: turning something round makes it face the other way, so the letters run backwards
first of picks out only the opening letter of the following word

blocks.note: an era is an age or epoch
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: The space age was switched on by the first Apollo missions.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'space age' as one phrase, but 'Space' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An area is an expanse or region of ground or surface, so it can stand for a stretch of space.

clue.text: Swimmer shockingly flashing around pier - not very good

indicators.note: something done shockingly is done in a wild, disordered way, so these letters are thrown about
not means without, so the named letters are taken away
going around something encloses it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged
taken as written
pi is crossword shorthand for pious, very good

explanation.surface: Someone swimming while exposing themselves near a pier behaves badly.
explanation.walkthrough: PI for pious, very good, is a crossword convention; removing it from the pier leaves just two letters for the scrambled word to surround.
explanation.definitionFit: An anglerfish is a sea fish, and any creature that moves through water can be called a swimmer in crosswords.

clue.text: City of Leipzig, in East Germany, evacuated at outset

indicators.note: the outset is the beginning, so only the opening letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of the city name
the opening letter of the word
the opening letter of the word
the opening letter of the country name
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A German city that was emptied of its people at the start of something.
explanation.walkthrough: Leipzig is a red herring for the answer city; 'evacuated' looks like an emptying instruction but is simply the last of the five words whose heads are taken.
explanation.definitionFit: Liège is a major city in eastern Belgium on the river Meuse.

clue.text: So, maybe Shrek's sent up

indicators.note: in a down entry, something sent up travels bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: Shrek, the animated film hero, is an ogre; 'maybe' marks him as one example

explanation.surface: So, it seems the Shrek film is being parodied.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sent up' reads as mocked or parodied, but in a down entry it means the letters run upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Ergo is Latin for 'therefore', used in English as a formal way of saying so or hence.

clue.text: Unpackaged setters' fags - nice, laid back smoke

indicators.note: laid back means placed backwards, so the run of words is read from the end
taking off the packaging removes the outer layer, leaving only the inner letters of each word

blocks.note: the word stripped of its first and last letters
the word without its outer letters
the word without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Loose cigarettes from the crossword setters, nice for a relaxed puff.
explanation.walkthrough: Fag is British slang for cigarette, which helps the surface. Trimming SETTERS, FAGS and NICE to their insides gives a sequence that, reversed, is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A smoke is a colloquial term for something to smoke, most often a single rolled tobacco product.

clue.text: Being led, struggling to win

indicators.note: struggling suggests writhing and twisting, so these letters wrestle into another order

blocks.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Trailing in a contest and battling to come out on top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being led' sounds like losing a race, but it describes something pulled along behind.
explanation.definitionFit: Something in tow is being pulled or followed along behind, so it is guided by whoever is in front.

clue.text: Prevents editor spinning the likes of Saddam

indicators.note: spinning turns something round to face the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: to stop something is to prevent it
ed is the usual abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: An editor is stopped from putting a favourable spin on dictators like Saddam Hussein.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spinning' suggests media spin, but it turns the whole phrase backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Saddam Hussein ruled Iraq as an absolute tyrant, so tyrants of his kind are despots.

clue.text: Rona Lee harassed another girl

indicators.note: someone harassed is flustered and thrown into disorder, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Rona Lee pestered a second young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another' refers back to 1 Across, whose answer is also a girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Eleanor is a female first name, so it is one more example of a name for a woman, after the first.
